Lai Study 1 replication with VH estimators

Technical review of historical comparability, reporting scale, and slope-SD diagnostics

Technical summary

This report reviews the Lai Study 1 data-generating mechanisms using the seven-method Vig–Hallquist Study 2 estimator bundle. It is designed to keep two questions separate:

  1. Can the overlapping methods reproduce the pattern in Lai’s Figure 2 under the historical scale and retention rule?
  2. What do all seven VH methods show when estimates are put on a common latent-slope-SD reporting scale and screened using the VH eligibility rule?

The historical Figure 2 panel is therefore a Figure 2 analogue, not an exact reproduction. The VH bundle does not contain Lai’s historical u1-only-EB and 2S-PAB variants, and Lai’s original standardization can vary by method. The diagnostic sections make that distinction inspectable rather than treating a scale change as an estimator effect.

The production aggregate contains 486 DGM conditions, 7 methods, and 2,430,000 simulated data sets per raw reporting view. Its source is /proj/mnhallqlab/projects/blup_unshrinking/outputs/lai_study1_vh_production_20260731/lai_study1_vh_summary.csv.

Result at a glance

For the historical comparison at (_{Zu1}=.4), the naïve dual-BLUP median trimmed bias is negative at every random-effect correlation (rho = -0.5: -0.022; rho = 0: -0.023; rho = 0.5: -0.021). Thus this VH implementation does not reproduce the correlation-signed naïve-EB pattern described for Lai’s Figure 2. In contrast, 2S-PA remains near zero (rho = -0.5: 0.000; rho = 0: -0.000; rho = 0.5: -0.000) and MSEM is small and positive (rho = -0.5: 0.002; rho = 0: 0.001; rho = 0.5: 0.000) on this historical view.

On the common latent-SD VH view, the naïve dual-BLUP median is not itself the main issue; its distribution has 11 conditions with (|| > 1), including a maximum of 5930.0. The report therefore shows its central behavior and its rare instability in separate panels rather than letting those failures flatten every other method’s plot.

Methods and terminology

The target is the effect of the level-2 covariate (Z) on the random slope (u_1). “Dual” means that the stage-2 regression uses both the random intercept (u_0) and random slope (u_1) as predictors; this is important when those random effects are correlated.

Estimator terminology used throughout this report
Method Stage-2 predictor or model Interpretive role
Oracle dual True simulated u0 and u1 Simulation benchmark; not available in applications
Naive dual BLUP Empirical-Bayes (BLUP) u0 and u1, treated as observed Shows attenuation/instability from ignoring first-stage uncertainty
Closed-form dual Closed-form corrected u0 and u1, treated as observed Separates corrected-score construction from stage-2 EIV correction
Fuller closed-form Closed-form corrected scores with their measurement-error covariance EIV-style correction using estimated first-stage error covariance
Fuller alpha-stepdown Fuller correction with alpha stepdown for a guarded correction Stabilized Fuller variant in the VH Study 2 bundle
2S-PA Lai two-stage path-analysis model fitted in OpenMx Direct Lai-method overlap for historical comparison
MSEM Joint multilevel structural-equation model fitted in Mplus Latent-variable benchmark and direct Lai-method overlap

The first three methods use a two-predictor observed-score regression in stage 2. The distinction is whether those predictors are true random effects, shrunken EB estimates, or closed-form corrected scores. The Fuller methods also propagate the estimated measurement-error covariance into the stage-2 correction. 2S-PA and MSEM instead fit their own latent-variable/path models, so their reported slope-SD scale must be interpreted separately in the historical comparison.

2. Historical Figure 2 analogue: compare like with like

This panel is the primary visual comparison with Lai’s Figure 2. It uses only the three overlapping methods (naive dual BLUP, 2S-PA, and MSEM), Lai’s method-specific historical standardization, Lai’s status_code == 0 retention rule, and a 20%-trimmed Monte Carlo bias. Those choices are deliberately different from the VH-primary analysis below.

Lai’s published Figure 2 code plots six methods: 2S-PA, 2S-PAB, MSEM, EB ((u_0+u_1)), centered EB, and uncentered EB. This analogue retains only the directly corresponding 2S-PA, MSEM, and dual-EB series; it cannot test the other three lines. The original plotting code is available in the Lai supplementary repository.

The key discrepancy is concentrated in the naïve dual-BLUP analogue: its median bias remains roughly (-.02) across (, 0, .5), instead of switching from negative to positive with the random-effect correlation as in the qualitative pattern reported for Lai’s Figure 2. This is evidence of a real implementation/DGM or estimand difference worth tracing; it is not explained away by the 2S-PA and MSEM lines, which remain close to zero on this historical view. Because the three omitted Lai series are not part of the VH bundle, this result narrows the discrepancy but does not establish an exact paper-level contradiction.

Historical coverage and Type I error analogues

The next two panels mimic Lai’s Figures 3 and 4 using the same three overlapping methods, historical scale, and status_code == 0 retention rule. Coverage is the proportion of retained 95% intervals containing the truth. The Type I panel is limited to (_{Zu1}=0) and uses two-sided 95% CI exclusion as the rejection rule. Lai’s original code used p < .05; these agree for ordinary two-sided Wald intervals but should not be called an exact p-value replication when an estimator’s interval construction differs.

The reference lines are .95 for coverage and .05 for Type I error. The table uses condition-level rates (not a pooled replication denominator), so it describes how performance varies across the Lai design. Interpret a departure from either reference together with the matching bias panel and the number of retained replications: a nominal interval result can change when the historical reporting multiplier or status-code retention changes.

If params$historical_figure_reference points to a locally saved image of the published Figure 2, render it alongside this panel during review. The visual comparison should ask whether the sign and correlation pattern agree, not whether the current all-method VH analysis matches a method-specific Lai scale.

The central-range panel shows that the closed-form dual estimator is the main source of systematic negative central bias when (_{Zu1}=.4), while the two Fuller estimators, 2S-PA, MSEM, and oracle are generally much closer to zero. The log-scale diagnostic adds the complementary fact that naïve dual BLUP has rare, severe failures even though its median is near zero. Neither claim is visible in the original unbounded all-method boxplot by itself.

4. Reporting-scale sensitivity: separate rescaling from estimator behavior

Raw and latent-SD rows report the same fitted estimator on different common condition-level scales. The historical standardized row is different: for the directly comparable methods it preserves Lai’s method-specific multiplier. Consequently, this section is a diagnostic of reporting conventions, not a competition between differently scaled numerical values.

Method-specific historical scaling diagnostics
method_label Mean Lai historical multiplier Availability
Naive dual BLUP 0.407 100.0%
2S-PA 0.493 100.0%
MSEM 0.475 100.0%

The key review question is whether an apparent change in bias survives the common latent-SD view. If it does not, the historical comparison is likely being driven partly by reporting scale rather than by a change in the fitted coefficient.

5. Slope-SD and reliability diagnostics: test the calibration explanation

The posterior reliability plotted here is calculated from the true full two-dimensional random-effect covariance and Lai’s RMS-scaled within-cluster design. It should not be replaced by lambda22 when random effects are correlated. The first plot makes the dependence on cluster size visible while retaining the remaining DGM variation as individual points.

True posterior slope reliability varies substantially within every homogeneous cluster-size level
clus_size Minimum reliability Median reliability Maximum reliability
3 0.073 0.465 0.862
10 0.208 0.731 0.953
25 0.397 0.867 0.981

The slope-SD ratios use the same Stage-1 fit attached to the naive dual BLUP raw summary, avoiding duplicate copies of the diagnostics across reporting views. A ratio of one is a diagnostic reference, not a convergence criterion.

The reliability result is consistent with cluster size being an important determinant, but rejects the stronger claim that it is merely a proxy for cluster size: at size 3 the reliability spans approximately .07–.86, and at size 25 it still spans approximately .40–.98. The EB slope SD is most attenuated at low reliability, whereas the fitted slope SD remains close to the population slope SD across the reliability range. This makes the slope-SD correction a useful diagnostic for the observed bias pattern rather than a substitute for modelling reliability itself.

6. Eligibility and convergence: compare the two retention rules directly

VH eligibility and original-Lai eligibility answer different questions. The historical rule retains runs with status_code == 0; the VH-primary rule also applies estimator-specific finite-estimate, finite-SE, design, and fit diagnostics. The following plot displays the average condition-level rate for each rule; it should accompany any comparison that changes the reporting scale or estimator bundle.

Condition-averaged eligibility overlap and convergence

Closed-form dual 100.0% 100.0% 5000.0 0.0 0.0 100.0%

2S-PA 89.3% 91.3% 4464.5 102.8 0.0 89.3%
MSEM 98.9% 98.9% 4946.0 0.0 0.0 98.9%

For this run, the VH screen is a strict subset of the original-Lai screen: there are no VH-only replications. The material differences occur for 2S-PA and naïve dual BLUP, for which about 2% of replications per condition are retained by the original status-code rule but excluded from the VH-primary analysis. Thus the rare large naïve-BLUP biases are not an artifact of a more permissive VH retention rule; the stricter VH screen is already in force.

Recommended review sequence

  1. Read the historical analogue beside Lai’s Figure 2, comparing sign and correlation patterns only for the three overlapping methods.
  2. Use the VH-primary panel to decide whether the low-reliability negative bias persists after common latent-SD reporting and VH eligibility.
  3. Consult the reporting-scale and slope-SD sections before attributing a cross-method bias difference to an estimator.
  4. Treat eligibility changes as part of the result: a discrepancy that appears only after a retention-rule change is not evidence of a DGM mismatch alone.

Reproducibility notes

The report is parameterized. After generating the Figure 2 post-processing outputs, render it from the repository root with:

quarto render reports/lai_study1_vh_review.qmd \
  -P results_dir:outputs/lai_study1_vh_production_20260731

Optionally supply figure_dir when figures live elsewhere and historical_figure_reference for a locally saved copy of Lai’s published Figure 2. This report does not rerun any models or alter the aggregate output.
